context.claim: On 1,200 held-out file-transfer problems balanced between permitted and forbidden requests, with four files and four recipients, linear decoders of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's final prompt-token residual state identify the requested file and its permitted recipient with at least 90% accuracy each, even among incorrect authorization decisions. Patching a fixed set of at most 12 attention heads from correct runs containing the same permission facts in reordered table rows corrects at least 30% of all initial errors while changing no more than 3% of correct decisions. Decoders, heads, and donor-selection rules are fixed on separate development data, with decoders trained on both correct and incorrect development runs; test names and permission assignments are unseen.

experiment_inputs.claim: On 1,200 held-out file-transfer problems balanced between permitted and forbidden requests, with four files and four recipients, linear decoders of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct's final prompt-token residual state identify the requested file and its permitted recipient with at least 90% accuracy each, even among incorrect authorization decisions. Patching a fixed set of at most 12 attention heads from correct runs containing the same permission facts in reordered table rows corrects at least 30% of all initial errors while changing no more than 3% of correct decisions. Decoders, heads, and donor-selection rules are fixed on separate development data, with decoders trained on both correct and incorrect development runs; test names and permission assignments are unseen.

claim_card.system: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct performing permission-based file-transfer authorization with four files and four recipients, evaluated using linear decoders of its final prompt-token residual state and a development-fixed attention-head patching pipeline.
claim_card.property: Requested-file and permitted-recipient decoding accuracies, measured separately on the full held-out test set and on initial authorization errors; percentage of all initial authorization errors corrected by attention-head patching; percentage of initially correct authorization decisions changed by the same intervention. Higher decoding accuracy and error-correction rate, and lower correct-decision change rate, are required.

conditions.task: File-transfer problems requiring authorization decisions from permission facts.
conditions.request_balance: The test set is balanced between permitted and forbidden requests: 600 of each.
conditions.test_split: The evaluation problems are held out from development data.
conditions.development_data: Separate development data are used to train and fix decoders and to select the heads and donor-selection rules.
conditions.unseen_test_names: Test names are unseen relative to development data.
conditions.unseen_test_permissions: Test permission assignments are unseen relative to development data.
conditions.decoder_type: Linear decoders for the requested file and its permitted recipient.
conditions.decoder_training_runs: Decoder training includes both correct and incorrect development runs.
conditions.decoder_fixation: Decoders are fixed on development data before held-out testing.
conditions.decoding_evaluation: Evaluate the same frozen decoders on all test problems and separately on all initially incorrect authorization cases, using original unpatched residual states.
conditions.head_selection: One attention-head set is selected on development data and fixed before testing.
conditions.donor_selection: Donor-selection rules are fixed on development data before testing.
conditions.donor_correctness: Donor runs make correct authorization decisions.
conditions.donor_permission_facts: Donor runs contain the same permission facts as the target runs.
conditions.donor_row_order: The donor permission-table rows are reordered.
conditions.error_correction_evaluation: Use all initially incorrect authorization decisions, identified before patching, as the correction-rate denominator; do not restrict evaluation to successfully patched cases.
conditions.correct_decision_evaluation: Use all initially correct authorization decisions as the decision-change denominator; measure authorization-decision changes rather than wording changes.
conditions.intervention_consistency: Use the same fixed patching intervention for error-correction and correct-decision preservation evaluations on the same test set.

claim_card.threshold: Requested-file accuracy and permitted-recipient accuracy must each be at least 90% on all 1,200 test problems (at least 1,080 correct predictions each), and each must separately be at least 90% among all initial authorization errors. The fixed patching intervention must correct at least 30% of all initial authorization errors while changing no more than 3% of initially correct authorization decisions. All six criteria must hold.
claim_card.comparator: For patching, the same model's initial, unpatched authorization decisions on the same held-out problems. Decoder predictions and authorization correctness are scored against task ground truth.
claim_card.state_phase: Inference and held-out evaluation, including residual-state decoding and inference-time attention-head patching.
claim_card.manipulation: Apply development-trained, frozen linear decoders to the original final prompt-token residual states. Patch one development-fixed set of at most 12 attention heads using activations from correct donor runs containing the same permission facts in reordered table rows, with donor-selection rules fixed on development data.
assumptions: Each problem has unambiguous ground truth for the requested file, its permitted recipient, and the correct authorization decision.
A prespecified label or readout mapping permits scoring decoder outputs consistently despite unseen test names.
Authorization decisions can be extracted and scored consistently, independently of superficial response wording.
Both the initially incorrect and initially correct subsets are nonempty, so all conditional accuracies and intervention rates have defined denominators.
Residual states and attention-head activations are accessible, and donor activations can be aligned with target runs despite table-row reordering.
Patched and unpatched runs are comparable apart from the stated intervention, with inference randomness controlled or accounted for.
Development/test separation and novelty checks are enforceable, and test results are not used to refit decoders or revise the selected heads or donor-selection rules.
A prespecified procedure establishes donor correctness and handles unavailable qualifying donors without removing initial errors from the correction-rate denominator.
free_variables: Exact problem-generation procedure, prompt template, table formatting, and distribution of unseen names and permission assignments within the stated setup.
Development-set size, composition, and sampling procedure, subject to including both correct and incorrect runs.
Residual-stream layer and normalization or readout convention at the final prompt-token position.
Decoder label encoding, feature preprocessing, training objective, regularization, and optimization settings.
Identities and layers of the fixed set of at most 12 attention heads.
Exact activation components and token positions patched, patching operation, and alignment across reordered table rows.
Donor-generation and fixed donor-selection algorithm, candidate row permutations, search budget, and handling of unavailable qualifying donors.
Any donor-request matching requirements beyond the explicitly shared permission facts.
Authorization-response format, decision-extraction protocol, and inference-generation settings.
Exact checkpoint revision, numerical precision, execution configuration, and random seeds.

experiment_inputs.scenario: Scenario (interp_1): Lack of adherence: Drift in long contexts, responses to knowledge conflict, incorrect tool use, bias. AI models when used in a task with long context and workflow can start begin to deviate from its originally specified goals and desired behaviors. These emergent behavior drifts are difficult to predict or detect and may lead to both value and goal misalignment. Interpretability research focuses on the characterization of underlying mechanisms and identification of root causes. Impact: Enable early detection of undesired behavior drifts and inform interventions to ensure AI system's persistent adherence to its intended value and goals over long workflow.. Research: Knowledge conflict detection and characterization,task/goal drift detection and mitigation, monitoring for persona shift and mitigation

observation_1.citation: Single model. All results are on Qwen3-30B-A3B. Cross-model transfer is untested.
observation_1.why: The April 8, 2026 primary report does not establish the requested thresholds. L2-regularized linear probes decode applicable/mismatch, not requested-file/permitted-recipient identities. Last-token residual results (layer: AUROC/accuracy): finance L40: 1.000/97.9%; code L28: .882/79.2%; vocabulary-controlled finance L40: .941/85.4%; code L32: .917/89.6%. Finance test: 48 examples, 24/class; training/development sizes and incorrect-decision decoding accuracy are unreported. Splits use unseen holder surface forms, reversed holder labels, and a held-out action; these do not establish unseen underlying entities or permission assignments. Separate development/test intervention selection is unspecified. Patches interchange full post_claim_context activations between examples differing only in claimed holder, not reordered rows. Correct-donor selection is unspecified. Finance mismatch→COMPLY: L16 15/36, L24 21/36, L28 14/36, L40 0/36; control-adjusted L24 16/34 (47%), with a differing denominator. Same-label controls: 0/36 applicable, 5/34 mismatch flips. Code L24: 12/34 forward, 6/35 reverse flips; net 10/34. Ticket-routing: initially 24/24 correct, then 12/12 mismatch flips and 0/12 reverse flips. These measure flips, not error repairs. L24 heads 25/28 were attention-readout candidates, not a fixed ≤12-head patch experiment. Neither ≥30% error correction nor ≤3% collateral changes is demonstrated; extrapolation to Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is unsupported.

tool_args_2.query: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct entity binding linear probes attention head patching reasoning errors
tool_args_2.context: Find primary research relevant to entity-binding decoding on incorrect decisions and selective causal repair in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Prioritize file-transfer permission tasks, but distinguish related tasks clearly. Extract whether linear probes decode requested entities and their associated recipients from the final prompt-token residual state on error subsets; whether a fixed small attention-head set repairs errors using semantically equivalent reordered-context donors; correction and collateral-change rates; and development/test separation. Do not treat probe accuracy as causal evidence or attention visualizations as successful patching.

observation_2.citation: “We fit a probe on a training fold, select its layer on a validation fold, and report results on a disjoint test fold.”
observation_2.why: Closest primary study of error-conditioned binding decoding and causal repair, but important mismatches remain: its task is entity–obligation retrieval, not file-transfer permission, and its 7B checkpoint is Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B, not Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Multinomial linear probes read the final query-position residual stream. For Qwen2.5-7B, failure-conditioned probe accuracy is 27.6% (seed range 23.6–34.5%), against a 12.5% present-obligation baseline. The decoding experiment uses 200 training, 200 validation, and 200 untouched test trials per seed, with refitting on training plus validation. Repair instead adds a class-mean residual direction toward the probe-decoded obligation; it does not patch a fixed attention-head set from reordered-context donors. In the separate repair configuration, Table 5 reports 29% error correction and 79% correct-trial preservation, implying 21% correct-to-incorrect collateral change; accuracy rises from 36.0% to 47.2%. Repair-layer selection uses validation failures, not test outcomes. Probe accuracy establishes decodability, while the intervention supplies separate causal evidence. These findings do not verify the requested recipient-decoding or selective head-repair claim.

observation_2.citation: “Through extensive experiments on nine models and ten binding tasks, we uncover a consistent pattern in how LMs mix these mechanisms to drive model behavior.”
observation_2.why: Primary research directly relevant to entity-binding mechanisms, including Qwen2.5-7B instruction-tuned experiments. It distinguishes positional, lexical, and reflexive retrieval routes using counterfactual activation interchange, rather than relying only on attention visualization. Binding information is studied through interventions on the last-token residual stream before retrieval. However, these are templated entity-retrieval tasks, including boxes and music, not file-transfer permission decisions. Counterfactual donors deliberately make retrieval mechanisms predict different entities; this is not evidence that semantically equivalent reordered-context donors selectively repair naturally incorrect decisions. The reported approximately 95% agreement concerns a causal model's prediction of next-token distributions, not an error-correction rate. The source does not establish the requested error-subset entity-and-recipient linear-probe results, a fixed small repair-head set, corresponding correction/collateral-change rates, or development/test separation for that repair protocol. Together with the first result, it supplies relevant binding research but leaves the specific file-transfer claim unverified.

tool_args_3.context: Seek primary experimental evidence matching a four-file, four-recipient permission-table task using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: 1,200 held-out balanced permitted/forbidden requests; linear final-prompt-token residual decoders for requested file and permitted recipient, including initially incorrect decisions; at most 12 fixed attention heads patched from correct runs with identical facts in reordered table rows. tool_args_4.query: language models entity attribute binding linear decoding small attention head circuits activation patching Feng Steinhardt
tool_args_4.context: Find primary experimental evidence about linearly accessible entity–attribute bindings and causal interventions through a small, fixed attention-head set. Prioritize Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct where available. Distinguish decoding at entity tokens from decoding at the final prompt token, and overall accuracy from accuracy conditioned on incorrect model answers. For interventions, extract head counts, whether the same heads are used across held-out examples, donor semantics, natural-error correction rates, and changes to initially correct answers. Counterfactual answer changes, artificial corruption recovery, or residual-vector steering are not equivalent to selective repair using semantically identical reordered-table donors. Report these distinctions explicitly. This is the final literature query; no experimental execution tool is available.

observation_4.citation: we collected hidden state activations at entity token positions as well as at final token positions at every layer
observation_4.why: Gur-Arieh, Geva and Geiger, Mixing Mechanisms, provides experiments including Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Appendix B.2 uses multinomial logistic regression at entity tokens and final tokens separately. Crucially, the decoded variable is entity-group position—not the complete entity–attribute binding. Middle positions become less separable as context grows. Counterfactual residual-stream interchange experiments distinguish positional, lexical and reflexive retrieval mechanisms; they are not small-head selective repair experiments. The paper does not report natural-error correction or initially-correct-answer damage for a fixed head set patched from semantically identical reordered-table donors. Its approximately 95% distributional agreement concerns a causal model of retrieval, not failure-conditioned decoding accuracy. Thus it supports accessible positional information and causal retrieval mechanisms, but not the stronger repair claim. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06182v1))

observation_4.citation: On the trials each model gets wrong, probe accuracy exceeds the strict present-obligation baseline, 1/K = 0.125
observation_4.why: Ravulapalli, Chadha and Hari, Legible Failures, directly tests binding decoding conditioned on incorrect answers, using final-query-position residual states and disjoint training, validation and test folds. The relevant checkpoint is Qwen2.5-7B BASE, not Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. For K=8, D=64, model accuracy is 57.1%; probe accuracy conditioned on model errors is 27.6% (seed range 23.6–34.5%), versus 12.5% chance. These are different quantities. In a separate K=6, D=256 steering experiment, Qwen2.5-7B accuracy rises from 36.0% to 47.2%; the decoded arm repairs 29% of wrong trials and preserves 79% of initially correct trials. The intervention changes residual vectors toward a probe-decoded binding; there is no attention-head set or reordered-table donor. Consequently, this is evidence for failure-conditioned accessibility and residual-steering repair, not selective repair through fixed heads. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.11216v1))

observation_4.citation: We further show that binding ID vectors form a continuous subspace
observation_4.why: Feng and Steinhardt, How do Language Models Bind Entities in Context?, is the foundational primary experimental source. It studies Pythia and LLaMA, not Qwen2.5. Entity- and attribute-position activation substitutions and additive mean interventions establish causally effective binding-ID directions; this is not a supervised final-prompt-token binding-decoding result. Interventions intentionally switch associations, erase binding information or restore artificially erased information. The reported above-97% accuracy when simultaneous entity and attribute interventions cancel is not a natural-error correction rate. The work neither identifies a small fixed attention-head set nor measures preservation of initially correct answers under reordered-table donor patching. Attention heads comparing binding IDs are explicitly proposed as a possible mechanism rather than experimentally isolated here. It supports linear/additive binding representations, not the complete selective-repair claim. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2310.17191v2))

observation_4.citation: consisting of a sparse set of 72 attention heads in four groups
observation_4.why: Prakash et al., Fine-Tuning Enhances Existing Mechanisms, supplies fixed-circuit evidence in Llama-7B and fine-tuned derivatives, not Qwen2.5. Circuit components are head–token-position pairs: groups operate at final, query-label and previous-query-label positions. The discovered 72-head circuit is evaluated without per-example reselection and transferred unchanged across models; separately discovered Goat/FLoat circuits contain 175 heads. The unchanged circuit retains 97%, 89% and 88% of full-model performance in Vicuna, Goat and FLoat respectively—faithfulness ratios, not percentages of natural errors repaired. Discovery uses original/noise pairs, semantic tests use counterfactual donors, and cross-model patching uses another model's activations on the same input. None is semantically identical reordered-table donor repair. The paper does not provide the requested wrong-to-correct and correct-to-wrong rates, nor establish them through entity-token versus final-token linear decoding. ([proceedings.iclr.cc](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/2082273791021571c410f41d565d0b45-Paper-Conference.pdf))

observation_4.citation: only 38 out of 672 attention heads (5.7%), are sufficient to recover most of the model’s rebinding behavior
observation_4.why: Oh and Demberg, A retrieval conditioned rebinding circuit, experimentally isolates model-level head sets in Gemma and Llama, not Qwen2.5. Gemma2-9B retains 38 heads with circuit accuracy 89% versus 100% full-model accuracy; Gemma3-12B retains 83/768 heads with 91% versus 100%; Llama3.2-3B retains 42/672 with 71% versus 71%; Llama3.1-8B retains 40/1024 with 84% versus 99%. These are circuit-performance evaluations, not natural-error repair rates. The study uses a selected circuit rather than example-specific head selection, but does not establish the requested held-out selective-repair protocol. Donor experiments alter objects or role-bearing tokens, and Q/K interventions redirect binding-ID matching. They therefore measure counterfactual routing and rebinding, not semantically identical reordered-table repair. Natural-error correction and damage to initially correct answers under that donor protocol are not reported; neither are failure-conditioned linear binding-decoding accuracies. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.08644v1))

hits.citation: “Steering the residual stream toward the probe-decoded binding, with no gold label, raises accuracy on all eight models tested”
hits.why: This is the primary paper matching the query. Its full text reports residual-stream steering rather than donor-based attention-head patching. Appendix D, Table 5 reports that Qwen2.5-7B repairs 29% of initially wrong trials and preserves 79% of initially correct trials at steering strength 0.5. Table 6 reports preservation falling to 69% and 61% at strengths 1.0 and 2.0. The checkpoint is Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B, not Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. The intervention uses six entity–obligation bindings and 1,200 total trials split into training, validation, and test folds—not 1,200 held-out file-transfer problems. Thus, this paper does not verify the contextual claim’s specific task, model, patching method, or thresholds.
